Motion sensors are only concerned with an object's rate of change and not position in space. For this reason, nearly all motion sensors are frequency devices, where output frequency is proportional to rate of change of motion...
The most popular motion sensors used in industry are the photo reflector, photo interrupter, and magnetic pickup. The devices sense surfaces, which repeatedly change during time intervals.

The motion of the photo interrupter surface must repeatedly make and break the light connection between the emitter and receiver. The motion of the photo reflector surface, allows light to reflect back to the receiver...

The magnetic pickup establishes a stationary field through a coil, called bias. When a moving magnetic material surface passes through the field, flux increases. The changing field will induce a current in the coil each time the surface moves...

Various surfaces are used on motion sensors. Repetitive surface changes occur as these surfaces move past the sensors, causing a pulse train at the outputs (optical receiver or coil) at the same rate as the motion...
The photo interrupter requires a surface that will alternately make and break the light path between emitter and receiver. It can be of any material that will block light.

The photo reflector sensor requires a surface that will alternately reflect and absorb (or pass) light. It must be of reflective material with holes or openings that will allow the light to pass without reflection...

The magnetic pickup requires a surface with changing magnetic permeability to change the bias, such as the presence or absence of a gear tooth near the pickup head. Sometimes small magnets are mounted on the moving surface...
The correlation of motion to frequency is accomplished by the moving surface and the sensor. The motion sensor correlates change in velocity to a frequency.

The motion sensor and surface pair can be a combination of any type. As the surface moves in front of an optical interrupter with a slotted disk, the interrupter alternately senses absence and presence of light...
As velocity is a function of distance and time, the frequency can be determined by first solving for velocity.

It is difficult to measure velocity directly from a waveform, as calculations are required. The purpose of sensor circuits is to convert the pulse train output of a sensor directly to an analog or digital readout...
The simplest motion circuit converts velocity to analog DC. In this circuit, velocity is proportional to a DC voltage or current. The integrated circuit below performs this function.

The motion sensor and surface pair can be a combination of any type. As the surface moves in front of an optical interrupter with a slotted disk, the interrupter alternately senses absence and presence of light...

The interrupter uses an LED phototransistor. The LED is properly biased by +Vcc and R1. The phototransistor is a biased common emitter, zero base bias. As the disk interrupts Q1 (light), Q1 collector outputs a pulse train...

The pulse train is wave shaped by A1 for the input to A2. The frequency to voltage (F/V) converter is an MSI chip that outputs a DC voltage in proportion to input frequency in V /Hz. This ratio is called conversion factor or CF.
The DC output of the frequency to voltage (F/V) converter chip may be read directly on a DC meter calibrated in distance per second.
Because the distance (D) between the interrupter slots, and the conversion factor of the F/V chip do not change, (D
CF) is a constant, and V is a function of velocity in units per second.

The sensing of rotary motion in RPM is perhaps the most popular application of motion sensors. Velocity in this application is relative and not absolute, as without a known circumference, run out or circular motion in distance per revolution cannot be computed...

This rotary motion application uses the same velocity sensing circuit as before, except the velocity (v) and RPM are directly proportional. One circuit may perform both functions by simply connecting two F/V chips to the buffer output, with one scaled for velocity and the other for RPM...

In measuring RPM, the distance (D) between the sensing edges is unimportant; it is only the number (N) of sensing marks which occur for each revolution (F ) of the rotating object that is significant..
